set1.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set1.q: A 44-year-old's lung-window computed tomography shows the trachea and main bronchi as dark circles. Why are they dark?
opts: They are filled with contrast
Contrast material is high attenuation and shows bright; it fills vessels, not the airways.
They are filled with air
Correct. Air and gas are low attenuation, so the air-filled trachea and bronchi show dark on computed tomography.
They are filled with fresh blood
Fresh blood from a hemorrhage is high attenuation (bright); dark airways mean air.
Their walls are calcified bone
Bone and calcium are very high attenuation and show bright, the opposite of the dark airways.

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 44-year-old man may have vasculitis. For this condition, which modality is superior to contrast computed tomography?
opts: Magnetic resonance imaging
Correct. Vasculitis is a contrast indication for computed tomography, although magnetic resonance is superior for it.
A ventilation/perfusion scan
A ventilation/perfusion scan looks for embolism; magnetic resonance is the superior study for vasculitis.
Pulmonary ultrasound
Pulmonary ultrasound is for trauma; magnetic resonance is the superior study for vasculitis.
A plain chest radiograph
A radiograph cannot assess vessel walls; magnetic resonance is the superior study for vasculitis.

set1.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set1.q: A 70-year-old with interstitial lung disease has this computed tomography slice. What pattern fills both lower lungs?
opts: Ground-glass opacities
Ground-glass opacities are hazy, pale areas of increased density, not clustered ring-like cysts.
Consolidation
Consolidation is dense, white filling of the lung, not clusters of air-filled rings.
Honeycombing
Correct. Clustered ring-like or cystic spaces, usually 3 to 10 millimeters, are honeycombing.
Pneumothorax
A pneumothorax is one black space outside a compressed lung, not many small cysts within it.
set1.alt: Transverse computed tomography slice of the chest

set1.io: Identify normal bony thoracic structures on chest radiographs.
set1.q: A 41-year-old woman's lung lobes are mapped onto her chest wall. Where do the inferior lobes lie?
opts: Above the fifth rib
Above the fifth rib are the superior lobes; the inferior lobes lie below the base of the fifth rib.
Below the second rib
The second rib marks the sternal angle; the dividing landmark for the lobes is the base of the fifth rib.
Below the tenth rib
The lung base reaches about the tenth posterior rib on inspiration; the inferior lobes begin below the fifth rib.
Below the fifth rib
Correct. Inferior to the base of the fifth rib are the inferior lobes; superior to it are the superior lobes.

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 49-year-old man asks how a ventilation/perfusion scan compares with a computed tomography angiogram for embolism. Which statement is correct?
opts: It is inferior to the angiogram
Correct. The ventilation/perfusion scan is inferior to the computed tomography angiogram and is done when the angiogram cannot be performed.
It is superior and is preferred first
That reverses it: the angiogram is first, and the ventilation/perfusion scan is the inferior alternative.
They are equivalent in every case
They are not equivalent; the ventilation/perfusion scan is inferior to the computed tomography angiogram.
It is the first test for trauma
Trauma uses pulmonary ultrasound for a collapsed lung or fluid; the ventilation/perfusion scan is for embolism.

set1.io: Identify abnormal chest imaging findings.
set1.q: A 40-year-old woman has this posteroanterior chest film. What technical problem does it show?
opts: Underexposure
An underexposed film is white, with small pulmonary vessels and no spine or mediastinal anatomy; this film is dark.
Overexposure
Correct. An overexposed film is dark: the thoracic spine, mediastinal structures and retrocardiac areas show through.
Poor inspiration
Poor inspiration leaves the diaphragm high with few posterior ribs above it; the problem here is how dark the film is.
Patient rotation
Rotation shows as uneven distances from the spinous processes to the clavicle borders, not as a dark film.

set1.io: Identify normal bony thoracic structures on chest radiographs.
set1.q: An 81-year-old woman's posteroanterior chest film is reviewed. How should the ribs be assessed?
opts: Over the painful area first
The read covers every rib one at a time on both sides, not just a painful area, so an unexpected fracture is not missed.
As a group, for overall shape
A glance at the overall shape misses a single rib's fracture; the read goes rib by rib, both sides, top to bottom.
On a separate lateral view
The ribs are assessed on the posteroanterior film itself, one at a time and bilaterally, moving inferiorly.
One by one, both sides, downward
Correct. Assess each rib one at a time, bilaterally, before moving inferiorly to the next one, comparing for symmetry.

set1.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set1.q: A 52-year-old woman has this routine posteroanterior chest radiograph. Which normal landmark does the arrow mark?
opts: The right cardiophrenic angle
The cardiophrenic angle is medial, where the right heart border meets the diaphragm; the arrow points to the lateral corner against the chest wall.
The right hilum
The right hilum sits mid-chest beside the heart, where the pulmonary vessels and bronchi enter, far above the diaphragm.
The right costophrenic angle
Correct. The costophrenic angle is the sharp V where the hemidiaphragm meets the lateral chest wall; normally it is sharp, and blunting suggests an effusion.
The horizontal fissure
The horizontal fissure runs across the mid right lung between the upper and middle lobes, not down at the base.
set1.alt: Posteroanterior chest radiograph with a yellow arrow

set1.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set1.q: A 40-year-old woman's lateral soft-tissue neck film shows no air in the esophagus behind the trachea. What does this mean?
opts: It suggests an esophageal obstruction
An airless esophagus is the expected appearance; it is collapsed between meals, so no obstruction is implied.
It suggests a retropharyngeal abscess
An abscess is a reason for computed tomography of the neck; an airless, collapsed esophagus is simply normal.
It is normal: the esophagus is collapsed
Correct. The esophagus shows no radiolucency because it is collapsed, which it should be when the patient is not eating.
It means the film is underexposed
Underexposure whitens the whole film and hides the spine. The esophagus is airless here because it is collapsed.

set1.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set1.q: A 45-year-old woman's posteroanterior film shows the left hilum slightly higher than the right. How should this be read?
opts: As left upper lobe collapse
Nothing else here suggests collapse. A left hilum sitting slightly above the right is the expected, normal arrangement.
As right hilar lymphadenopathy
Hila are checked for masses and lymphadenopathy, but those change size and density. The left being higher is the normal pattern.
As a normal finding
Correct. The left hilum is normally slightly higher than the right; the two should be concave and similar in size and density.
As a rotated film
Rotation is judged from the spinous processes to the clavicle borders, not from hilar height; the left hilum is normally the higher one.

mis.As left upper lobe collapse: pathology read into a normal variant
mis.As a rotated film: technique read into a normal variant

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 58-year-old woman's computed tomography angiogram is read for a thrombus. Which vessels matter most?
opts: The pulmonary veins
The pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium; for an embolism the pulmonary arteries are the concern.
The descending aorta
The descending aorta is an orientation landmark beside the spine; emboli lodge in the pulmonary arteries.
The ascending aorta
The ascending aorta is a landmark beside the main pulmonary artery; for an embolism the pulmonary arteries matter most.
The pulmonary arteries
Correct. When assessing for an embolism or thrombus, the pulmonary arteries are of the greatest concern.

set1.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set1.q: A 58-year-old woman's heart size is judged on a posteroanterior film. What is the most the heart should span?
opts: One third of the chest width
One third is not the limit. The heart should not be more than half the posteroanterior span of the chest.
Half of the chest width
Correct. On a posteroanterior view the heart should not be more than one half of the span of the chest.
Two thirds of the chest width
Two thirds is too much: the upper limit of a normal heart is half the posteroanterior span of the chest.
Three quarters of the chest width
Three quarters would be a markedly enlarged heart; the normal heart spans no more than half the chest.

set1.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set1.q: A 30-year-old woman has a skull radiograph. What are the symmetrical dark pockets above and beside the orbits?
opts: Vascular grooves
A vascular groove is a thin line on the lateral skull, where the middle meningeal artery runs, not a pocket beside the orbits.
Fracture lines
Bones are checked for continuity, and a fracture is a line that should not be there; paired dark pockets are the sinuses.
Air-filled sinuses
Correct. The airways and the air-filled sinus cavities are radiolucent, so they show dark; note them and check for symmetry.
The sella turcica
The sella turcica is a single midline bony saddle seen on the lateral view, not paired pockets beside the orbits.

set1.io: Identify normal bony thoracic structures on chest radiographs.
set1.q: A clinician palpates the sternal angle of a 50-year-old to count ribs before a procedure. Which rib joins the sternum here?
opts: The first rib
The first rib is above the sternal angle, at the top of the chest; the sternal angle marks the second rib.
The second rib
Correct. The sternal angle (manubriosternal joint) communicates with the second rib, the starting point for counting ribs.
The third rib
The third rib is one below; the sternal angle (the manubriosternal joint) marks the second rib.
The fifth rib
The fifth rib is lower, near the nipple line; the sternal angle marks the second rib.

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 24-year-old arrives in the trauma bay after a car crash. Which bedside study quickly checks for a collapsed lung?
opts: A ventilation/perfusion scan
A ventilation/perfusion scan is a nuclear study for pulmonary embolism, not a bedside trauma check.
Positron emission tomography
Positron emission tomography looks for cancer metastases; it has no role in a trauma bay.
Pulmonary ultrasound
Correct. Pulmonary ultrasound is used almost exclusively in trauma to assess for a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) or fluid, as part of the extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma.
Magnetic resonance imaging
Magnetic resonance is not a bedside study and has few primary pulmonary indications; ultrasound is used in the trauma bay.

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 40-year-old outpatient walks into radiology for a chest film. Which view is taken standing, with the beam entering from behind?
opts: Posteroanterior
Correct. The posteroanterior view is taken with the patient upright and ambulatory; the anteroposterior view is taken supine and magnifies the heart.
Anteroposterior
The anteroposterior view is the supine one, often in bed, and it magnifies the heart.
Lateral
A lateral film is taken from the side, showing the retrosternal and retrocardiac spaces; it is not the front-to-back view.
Water's view
The Water's view is a skull film angled 45 degrees to the orbitomeatal line for the sinuses.

set1.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set1.q: A 58-year-old with fever and a productive cough has this computed tomography slice. What does the right lung show?
opts: Consolidation
Correct. The dense, white filling of part of the right lung on computed tomography is consolidation, the pneumonia pattern.
Pneumothorax
A pneumothorax is black air outside a compressed lung; here part of the lung itself is filled in.
Honeycombing
Honeycombing is clustered ring-like cysts of interstitial lung disease, not a dense filled-in area.
Pleural effusion
An effusion collects in the pleural space outside the lung; here the lung tissue itself is filled in.
set1.alt: Transverse computed tomography slice of the chest

set1.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set1.q: A 33-year-old has sudden chest pain and this transverse computed tomography. What does it show on the left?
opts: A large pleural effusion
An effusion is gray fluid; this space is black air, the darkest density on the scan.
Lobar consolidation
Consolidation is white filling of lung tissue; here the lung is pushed away by black air.
Honeycombing
Honeycombing is clustered ring-like cysts within the lung, not one large black space around it.
A pneumothorax
Correct. Black air fills the left pleural space and compresses the left lung toward the back: a pneumothorax.
set1.alt: Transverse computed tomography slice of the chest with yellow and red arrows and the words removed

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 70-year-old man's staging scan is ordered as a combined study. Why is positron emission tomography now mostly done with computed tomography?
opts: It removes the radiation dose
Both parts use radiation; the reason for combining them is a much clearer image.
The combined image is much clearer
Correct. Positron emission tomography is now done mostly as a combined scan with computed tomography, which gives a much clearer image.
It replaces the need for contrast
Contrast decisions are separate; the combination is done because it gives a much clearer image.
It costs less than either alone
Positron emission tomography is already the more expensive nuclear scan; the combination is chosen for clarity.

set1.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set1.q: A 61-year-old has this transverse computed tomography angiogram of the chest. What does the arrow mark?
opts: The ascending aorta
The ascending aorta is anterior, beside the main pulmonary artery near the sternum, not back against the spine.
The left pulmonary artery
The left pulmonary artery branches from the main pulmonary artery toward the left hilum; it does not sit round beside the spine.
The left atrium
The left atrium is the chamber the pulmonary veins drain into; the round vessel beside the spine is the descending aorta.
The descending aorta
Correct. The descending aorta is the round, brightly lit vessel beside the vertebral column, always on the patient's left.
set1.alt: Transverse computed tomography angiogram of the chest with a yellow arrow

set1.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set1.q: A 34-year-old man has this standing posteroanterior chest radiograph for a job physical. What does the arrow point to?
opts: The aortic knob
Correct. The rounded bulge at the top of the left mediastinal border is the aortic knob, the aortic arch seen end-on; it is a landmark to find on every film.
The pulmonary trunk
The pulmonary trunk (pulmonary artery) sits just below the aortic knob on the left mediastinal border, not at the top of it.
The left hilum
The left hilum is lower, in the middle of the lung field where the pulmonary vessels and bronchi enter; it bisects the chest.
The left ventricle
The left ventricle forms the lower left heart border down to the diaphragm, well below the bulge the arrow marks.
set1.alt: Posteroanterior chest radiograph with a yellow arrow

mis.The pulmonary trunk: adjacent structure on the same border
mis.The left ventricle: adjacent structure on the same border

set1.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set1.q: A 68-year-old with dyspnea has this transverse computed tomography. What does it show in the right chest?
opts: A large pleural effusion
Correct. A large gray collection fills the right pleural space and compresses the right lung: a pleural effusion on computed tomography.
A pneumothorax
A pneumothorax would be black air, the darkest density; this collection is gray fluid.
Lobar consolidation
Consolidation fills the lung tissue itself; this is a gray collection outside the compressed lung.
Honeycombing
Honeycombing is clustered ring-like cysts within the lung, not a smooth gray collection in the pleural space.
set1.alt: Transverse computed tomography slice of the chest

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 59-year-old long-term smoker is seen in clinic. Which finding is a listed indication for a chest radiograph?
opts: Unexplained weight loss
Correct. Unexplained weight loss in any chronic smoker is an indication for a chest radiograph.
A muffled voice
A muffled voice is an indication for a soft-tissue neck radiograph, not for a chest film.
Suspected sinus infection
Suspected sinus infection points to a Water's view of the sinuses, not a chest radiograph.
Anterior neck pain
Anterior neck pain is an indication for a soft-tissue neck radiograph, not a chest radiograph.

set1.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set1.q: A 76-year-old woman's chest radiograph shows Kerley B lines. What causes them?
opts: Fluid in the pleural space
Fluid in the pleural space is an effusion, which blunts the costophrenic angles; Kerley B lines come from thickened septa.
Thickened interlobular septa
Correct. Kerley B lines are caused by thickening of the interlobular septa, the walls separating the tiny lobules of the lung.
Air in the pleural space
Air in the pleural space is a pneumothorax; Kerley B lines come from thickened interlobular septa.
Airways pulled open by fibrosis
Airways pulled open by fibrotic pull are traction bronchiectasis; Kerley B lines are thickened interlobular septa.

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 66-year-old man asks about the risks of his chest radiograph. What are its true contraindications?
opts: There are none
Correct. Radiographs have no true contraindications; dose is limited over a lifetime, pregnancy is checked, and sensitive organs are shielded.
Pregnancy
Pregnancy is not an absolute contraindication; a pregnancy test is ordered and the fetus is shielded.
Any contrast allergy
A plain radiograph uses no contrast, so a contrast allergy does not apply; radiographs have no true contraindications.
A cardiac pacemaker
Support hardware such as a pacemaker is an indication for a chest radiograph, to evaluate it, not a contraindication.

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in the emergency department may have a pulmonary embolism. Which statement about imaging applies?
opts: Imaging is absolutely contraindicated
Imaging modalities have few to no true contraindications; pregnancy is a caution, and emergent studies are still done.
Done if emergent, even with contrast
Correct. Pregnancy is a caution, not an absolute contraindication: in emergent situations, such as pulmonary embolism, imaging is done, even with contrast.
Imaging waits until delivery
Emergent imaging is not delayed in pregnancy; it is done when needed, even with contrast, as for a pulmonary embolism.
Contrast is ruled out
In emergent situations imaging in pregnancy is done even with contrast, so contrast is not ruled out.

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 47-year-old had anaphylaxis to shellfish and has never been tested for an iodine allergy. How should this history be treated?
opts: A reason to avoid plain radiographs
Plain radiographs use no contrast, so this history does not bear on them; it is a caution before iodinated contrast.
A caution before magnetic resonance
Magnetic resonance contrast is gadolinium, not iodine; the shellfish history is listed as a caution before iodinated contrast.
A caution before iodinated contrast
Correct. Anaphylaxis to shellfish, not yet tested for iodine allergy versus the shellfish itself, is listed as a caution for contrast.
A caution before pulmonary ultrasound
Pulmonary ultrasound uses no contrast, so this history does not bear on it; it is a caution before iodinated contrast.

set1.io: Identify abnormal chest imaging findings.
set1.q: The posterior ribs above the diaphragm are counted on this frontal chest film of a 72-year-old. What does the count show?
opts: An adequate inspiration
Adequate inspiration brings the domes to the tenth posterior rib standing (eighth to tenth seated or lying), not the sixth.
Overexposure
Overexposure is about how dark the film is; the rib count measures inspiration.
Patient rotation
Rotation is judged from the spinous processes to the clavicle borders; counting ribs measures inspiration.
Poor inspiratory effort
Correct. Only six posterior ribs show above the diaphragm; a good inspiration brings the domes down to the tenth posterior rib standing, or the eighth to tenth seated or lying.
set1.alt: Posteroanterior chest radiograph with two posterior ribs numbered in yellow

set1.io: Identify abnormal chest imaging findings.
set1.q: A 45-year-old's posteroanterior film shows the trachea pushed to one side. How should this be read?
opts: As normal on an anteroposterior film
The view changes heart size, not tracheal position; the trachea should be midline on every film.
As normal in older adults
Age does not make deviation normal; the trachea should be midline.
As a sign of underexposure
Underexposure whitens the film; it does not move the trachea, which should sit in the midline.
As abnormal: the trachea should be midline
Correct. The trachea is checked as midline or deviated, and it should be midline; deviation is an abnormal finding.

set1.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 49-year-old has this computed tomography image of the chest. In which plane is it displayed?
opts: Frontal (coronal)
A frontal image runs head to foot and shows the lungs from apex to diaphragm; this is a cross-section.
Sagittal
A sagittal image shows one side in profile, front to back; this cross-section shows both lungs.
Transverse (axial)
Correct. A transverse (axial) image is a cross-section: both lungs, the airways, the mediastinum and the vertebra at the bottom.
A posteroanterior radiograph
A radiograph superimposes everything; this is a computed tomography slice in cross-section.
set1.alt: Computed tomography image of the chest

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 26-year-old woman needs a chest radiograph for a cough. What must be done before it is taken?
opts: A pregnancy history alone
History is not enough: the test itself (beta human chorionic gonadotropin, urine or blood) is ordered every time.
A serum creatinine level
Creatinine matters before contrast, which a plain radiograph does not use; the required step here is a pregnancy test.
Computed tomography instead
Computed tomography delivers more radiation, not less, and the radiograph is first line; the step is a pregnancy test.
A urine or blood pregnancy test
Correct. Always order a beta human chorionic gonadotropin urine or blood test on every female of potential childbearing age.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman needs a procedure guided by pulmonary ultrasound. What are the contraindications to it?
opts: Pregnancy
Pregnancy is a caution for computed tomography and nuclear studies; pulmonary ultrasound has no contraindications.
There are none
Correct. Pulmonary ultrasound has no contraindications, and it can also be used to guide procedures.
A non-titanium metal implant
Non-titanium metal implants are a precaution for magnetic resonance; pulmonary ultrasound has none.
An allergy to contrast
Contrast allergy matters for contrast computed tomography; pulmonary ultrasound uses no contrast and has no contraindications.

set2.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set2.q: A 3-month-old has this chest film; a yellow line outlines one region and a red line another. What does the yellow outline enclose?
opts: Air outside the lung (pneumothorax)
Correct. The yellow outline marks the pneumothorax, jet black on the radiograph; the red outline marks the compressed right lung.
Fluid in the pleural space
Fluid would be white or gray and blunt the base; the outlined area is jet black, which is air.
Consolidation of the right lung
Consolidation is white filling of the lung; the outlined area is black and has no lung in it.
Normal aerated right lung
The aerated lung is what the red outline marks, compressed toward the midline; the yellow area is air outside it.
set2.alt: Frontal chest radiograph of an infant with a yellow and a red outline drawn on the right side

set2.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set2.q: A 29-year-old man's lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph is read. Which space holds the esophagus?
opts: The retrotracheal space
Correct. The retrotracheal space, behind the trachea, is where the esophagus lies on the lateral neck film.
The nasopharyngeal space
The nasopharyngeal space is at the top of the airway behind the nose, well above the esophagus.
The retrosternal space
The retrosternal space is behind the sternum on a lateral chest film, not part of the neck film.
The vallecula
The vallecula is the pocket between the tongue base and the epiglottis, not the space behind the trachea.

set2.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set2.q: A 6-year-old has noisy breathing and a lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph. Which structure appears as the dark column in front of the cervical spine?
opts: The esophagus
The esophagus lies behind the trachea and shows no radiolucency because it is collapsed, as it should be when not eating.
The epiglottis
The epiglottis is a soft-tissue structure, not an air column; the air-filled trachea is the dark, radiolucent one.
The hyoid bone
The hyoid is bone, so it is radiopaque (bright). Air in the trachea makes the dark column.
The trachea
Correct. The trachea is patent and full of air, so it is radiolucent (dark) on the lateral neck film.

set2.io: Identify normal bony thoracic structures on chest radiographs.
set2.q: A 33-year-old man's lateral neck film is used to locate the larynx. Between which vertebral levels does it lie?
opts: C1 to C3
C1 to C3 is too high in the neck; the larynx lies lower, from the third to the sixth cervical vertebra (C3 to C6).
C3 to C6
Correct. The larynx spans the third to the sixth cervical vertebra (C3 to C6) on the lateral neck film.
C6 to T1
C6 to T1 is too low; the larynx spans C3 to C6, and the trachea continues below it.
T1 to T4
T1 to T4 is thoracic; the larynx is in the neck, from C3 to C6.

set2.io: Identify abnormal chest imaging findings.
set2.q: A 78-year-old in the intensive care unit has a supine anteroposterior chest film, and the heart looks large. What should be considered first?
opts: The view magnifies the heart
Correct. The anteroposterior view, taken supine, magnifies the heart, so the view must be known before calling the heart enlarged.
Cardiomegaly is confirmed
Not on this view alone: the anteroposterior film magnifies the heart, so its size is read with that in mind.
The film is overexposed
Overexposure darkens the film; it does not enlarge the heart. The supine anteroposterior view does.
The patient is rotated
Rotation shows as uneven spinous-process-to-clavicle distances; the large heart here comes from the anteroposterior view.

set2.io: Identify abnormal chest imaging findings.
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman's posteroanterior film is checked for rotation. How is rotation best assessed?
opts: The position of the tracheal shadow
Do NOT use the tracheal shadow; rotation is measured from the spinous processes to the clavicle borders.
The height of each hemidiaphragm
Diaphragm height reflects inspiration; rotation is measured from the spinous processes to the clavicles.
The number of posterior ribs seen
Counting posterior ribs measures inspiration; rotation is measured from the spinous processes to the clavicles.
Spinous processes to each clavicle border
Correct. Rotation is best assessed by measuring the distance between the central spinous processes and the borders of the clavicles.

set2.io: Identify abnormal chest imaging findings.
set2.q: A 44-year-old man has this posteroanterior chest film. What technical problem does it show?
opts: Underexposure
Correct. An underexposed film is white: small pulmonary vessels, and no spine or mediastinal anatomy can be seen.
Overexposure
An overexposed film is dark, with the thoracic spine and retrocardiac areas showing through; this film is white.
Poor inspiration
Poor inspiration leaves the diaphragm high over few posterior ribs; the problem here is a washed-out white film.
Patient rotation
Rotation shows as uneven distances from the spinous processes to the clavicles, not as a white film.

set2.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set2.q: A 79-year-old with heart failure has this posteroanterior film. What do the purple arrows mark?
opts: Kerley B lines
Correct. Kerley B lines are short, thin, horizontal lines at the outer edges of the lower lungs, from thickened interlobular septa.
Cephalization of vessels
Cephalization is marked by the green arrows: prominent vessels in the upper lungs.
A pleural effusion
The effusion is marked by the yellow arrow at the right base; the purple arrows point to horizontal lines at the edge.
Honeycombing
Honeycombing is ring-like cystic spaces of interstitial lung disease, not short horizontal lines.
set2.alt: Posteroanterior chest radiograph with green, yellow, purple and red markers and the words removed

set2.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set2.q: A 50-year-old woman's posteroanterior film is normal. Where does each hilum lie vertically?
opts: Level with the clavicles at the apex
The clavicles cross the lung apices; the hila sit much lower, halfway down the lung, where they bisect the chest.
Just above the hemidiaphragms
The diaphragm is the lung base. The hila sit halfway between apex and base, with equal lung above and below.
At the top of the aortic knob
The aortic knob is the upper left mediastinal bulge; the pulmonary artery lies below it and the hilum lower still, mid-chest.
Midway, with equal lung above and below
Correct. The hilum bisects the chest: about as much lung lies above it as below it.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 41-year-old has this computed tomography reconstruction of the chest. In which plane is it displayed?
opts: Sagittal
A sagittal image shows only one lung in profile, front to back, with the spine along one side.
Transverse (axial)
A transverse image is a cross-section like a slice of bread, viewed from the feet, with the sternum at the top.
Frontal (coronal)
Correct. A frontal (coronal) image shows both lungs side by side from apex to base, as if facing the patient.
A posteroanterior radiograph
A radiograph superimposes everything; this is a computed tomography slice with no overlying ribs blurring the lungs.
set2.alt: Computed tomography image of the chest

set2.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set2.q: A 61-year-old man's posteroanterior film is checked with the one-third, two-thirds rule. How should the heart sit across the midline?
opts: Two thirds right of midline, one third left
That reverses the rule. The heart sits mostly to the patient's left: one third right of the midline, two thirds left.
Half on each side of the midline
The heart is not centered. The rule is one third to the right of the midline and two thirds to the left.
Entirely left of the vertebral column
Part of the heart (the right atrium border) lies right of the midline; the split is one third right, two thirds left.
One third right of midline, two thirds left
Correct. On a normal posteroanterior film one third of the heart lies to the right of the midline and two thirds to the left.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 62-year-old woman with cancer has the study shown. Which study is it?
opts: A ventilation/perfusion scan
A ventilation/perfusion scan shows only the two lungs in several views, in gray, not a fused whole-body image.
A computed tomography angiogram
An angiogram is a gray-scale scan with bright, contrast-filled vessels, not a color fusion and whole-body uptake view.
Magnetic resonance imaging
Magnetic resonance images are gray-scale T1 or T2 slices, not a color fusion with a whole-body uptake view.
Positron emission tomography
Correct. A fused color slice with a whole-body view of tracer uptake is positron emission tomography, here combined with computed tomography.
set2.alt: Two-panel nuclear medicine study: a color transverse slice and a whole-body projection

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 63-year-old has this contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography. What does the arrow show?
opts: Normal contrast in the right pulmonary artery
Normal contrast fills the artery evenly and brightly; the arrow marks a dark defect within it.
Air in the right main bronchus
Air in a bronchus is dark but lies in the airway; the arrow is on the contrast-filled artery.
A right hilar lymph node mass
Hila are checked for masses, but the arrow marks a defect inside the bright pulmonary artery itself.
A clot in the right main pulmonary artery
Correct. The arrow marks a dark filling defect inside the bright, contrast-filled right main pulmonary artery: a clot.
set2.alt: Transverse contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest with a white arrow

set2.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set2.q: A 66-year-old with worsening shortness of breath has this posteroanterior film with a diffuse pattern through both lungs. Which condition fits?
opts: A right pneumothorax
A pneumothorax is a jet-black space with the lung compressed, not a diffuse pattern through both lungs.
Bilateral pleural effusions
An effusion blunts the costophrenic angles at the bases; it does not create a diffuse pattern through the lungs.
Interstitial lung disease
Correct. Interstitial lung disease typically shows a diffuse, abnormal pattern affecting the lung tissue (the interstitium) on the radiograph.
A normal chest film
A normal film shows clear, dark lungs with only the vascular markings; this pattern is diffuse and abnormal.

set2.io: Identify normal bony thoracic structures on chest radiographs.
set2.q: A 38-year-old woman's neck is examined before imaging. Which structures does the posterior triangle contain?
opts: The carotid bifurcation
The bifurcation of the common carotid artery is in the carotid triangle, part of the anterior triangle.
The trachea and larynx
The trachea and larynx are midline, deep to the jugular notch and laryngeal prominence, not in the posterior triangle.
Subclavian vein, lung apices
Correct. The posterior triangle of the neck contains the subclavian vein and the lung apices.
The hyoid and epiglottis
The hyoid and epiglottis are anterior midline structures of the upper airway, not posterior-triangle contents.

set2.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set2.q: A 59-year-old man's transverse computed tomography angiogram shows four chambers. Which feature identifies the left ventricle?
opts: It lies against the sternum
The chamber against the sternal wall is the right ventricle; the left ventricle is recognized by its thick wall.
It has the thickest wall
Correct. The left ventricle always has the thickest wall compared with the right ventricle.
It receives the pulmonary veins
The pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium, not the left ventricle, whose marker is the thickest wall.
It lies right of the vertebral column
The heart sits more to the patient's left; the left ventricle is identified by its wall thickness.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 63-year-old man's ventilation/perfusion scan has been read. How is the result reported?
opts: As positive or negative for clot
The scan is not a yes-or-no test; the result is a low, medium or high probability of pulmonary embolism.
As a low, medium or high probability
Correct. The ventilation and perfusion images are compared, and the result is a low, medium or high probability of pulmonary embolism.
As an attenuation value
Attenuation describes computed tomography; the ventilation/perfusion result is a probability of embolism.
As a T1 and T2 signal
T1 and T2 describe magnetic resonance; the ventilation/perfusion result is a low, medium or high probability.

set2.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman's chest film has been scanned through both lung fields. Which two spaces are assessed next?
opts: The retropharyngeal and retrotracheal spaces
Those are spaces on a lateral soft-tissue neck film. On the chest film the next spaces are retrosternal and retrocardiac.
The nasopharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces
Those belong to the soft-tissue neck film; the chest read moves from the lung fields to the retrosternal and retrocardiac spaces.
The retrosternal and retrocardiac spaces
Correct. After the lung fields, which should be radiolucent because they are filled with air, assess the retrosternal and retrocardiac spaces.
The subphrenic and paraspinal spaces
Those are not the next step. After the lung fields the read assesses the retrosternal and the retrocardiac spaces.

set2.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set2.q: A 5-year-old has fever and a cough, and this radiograph is taken. What is the term for the white areas filling the lungs?
opts: Honeycombing
Honeycombing is ring-like cystic spaces of interstitial lung disease, best seen on computed tomography, not white filling.
Consolidation
Correct. Pneumonia shows as consolidation: white, filled-in lung where the air-filled lung should be dark.
Kerley B lines
Kerley B lines are short, thin horizontal lines at the lung edges in edema, not filled-in white lung.
Pneumothorax
A pneumothorax is jet black on a radiograph, the opposite of white filling.
set2.alt: Frontal chest radiograph of a child

set2.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set2.q: A 70-year-old's chest computed tomography angiogram is confusing to read. Where does the descending aorta always lie?
opts: Left of the patient's vertebral column
Correct. If you lose your orientation, find the descending aorta: it is always on the left side of the patient's vertebral column.
Right of the patient's vertebral column
That reverses it. The descending aorta always lies on the patient's left of the vertebral column.
Directly behind the sternum
Behind the sternum is the right ventricle; the descending aorta is posterior, beside the spine on the left.
Between the two ventricles
The septum lies between the ventricles; the descending aorta is the round vessel beside the vertebral column on the left.

set2.io: Identify normal pulmonary structures on radiographic imaging.
set2.q: A 47-year-old man has this standing posteroanterior chest radiograph. What does the arrow beneath the left hemidiaphragm point to?
opts: The liver
The liver lies under the right hemidiaphragm, and it is soft tissue density rather than a dark pocket of gas.
The gastric bubble
Correct. Gas in the stomach shows as a dark bubble under the left hemidiaphragm; it is normal and is one of the landmarks to know.
The left costophrenic angle
The left costophrenic angle is the sharp lateral corner where the diaphragm meets the chest wall, not a gas pocket under the dome.
The left cardiophrenic angle
The cardiophrenic angle is where the heart border meets the diaphragm, above the dome rather than beneath it.
set2.alt: Posteroanterior chest radiograph with a yellow arrow

set2.io: Identify normal bony thoracic structures on chest radiographs.
set2.q: A 36-year-old man is examined for landmarks before reading his chest film. Which intercostal space does the nipple line mark?
opts: The third
The third intercostal space is higher; the nipple line corresponds to the fifth.
The fourth
The fourth intercostal space is one too high; the nipple line marks the fifth.
The fifth
Correct. The nipple line corresponds to the fifth intercostal space.
The sixth
The sixth intercostal space is one too low; the nipple line marks the fifth.

set2.io: Recognize common imaging findings associated with: Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, Pneumothorax, Interstitial lung disease
set2.q: A 74-year-old with shortness of breath has this posteroanterior film. What is the key finding at the lung bases?
opts: Kerley B lines
Kerley B lines are short horizontal lines at the outer edges of the lower lungs; the bases here are filled in and blunted.
Honeycombing
Honeycombing is ring-like cystic spaces on computed tomography in interstitial lung disease, not blunted angles.
Blunted costophrenic angles
Correct. The costophrenic angles have lost their sharp V on both sides: blunting, the hallmark of pleural effusion.
A visible lung edge with black space
A lung edge with jet-black space beyond is pneumothorax; here the bases are white and blunted.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 52-year-old with suspected pulmonary embolism had anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast. Which study is the alternative?
opts: A ventilation/perfusion scan
Correct. The ventilation/perfusion scan is done when a computed tomography angiogram cannot be performed, primarily for contrast allergy.
A computed tomography angiogram
The angiogram needs iodinated contrast, which this patient cannot have; the ventilation/perfusion scan is the alternative.
Positron emission tomography
Positron emission tomography looks for metastases, not pulmonary embolism.
Pulmonary ultrasound
Pulmonary ultrasound is used in trauma for a collapsed lung or fluid, not to find an embolism.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 55-year-old man has two days of chest pain and shortness of breath. Which imaging study comes first?
opts: Computed tomography of the chest
Computed tomography is usually secondary, ordered when the radiograph is inconclusive; it comes first only for suspected pulmonary embolism.
A chest radiograph
Correct. Chest radiographs are almost always the first-line study for a pulmonary or cardiac complaint, and pain and dyspnea are their main indications.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the chest
Magnetic resonance has few primary pulmonary indications and is not first line; the chest radiograph is.
A ventilation/perfusion scan
A ventilation/perfusion scan looks for pulmonary embolism when an angiogram cannot be done; it is not the first study for chest pain.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 39-year-old woman's chest magnetic resonance report describes an inflamed area. How does inflammation appear on the two main weightings?
opts: Dark on T1, bright on T2
Correct. Inflammation is dark on T1 and bright on T2; fat, by contrast, is bright on T1, and air is always dark.
Bright on T1, dark on T2
That reverses it. Inflammation is dark on T1 and bright on T2; fat is the tissue that is bright on T1.
Dark on both T1 and T2
Air is the thing that is always very dark; inflammation turns bright on T2.
Bright on both T1 and T2
Inflammation is not bright on T1; it is dark on T1 and bright on T2.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with cancer needs her neck lymph nodes checked for metastases. Which computed tomography fits best?
opts: Computed tomography without contrast
Lymph node metastases are a listed indication for contrast; a plain scan may miss what contrast shows.
A low-dose screening scan
Cancer screening is a separate computed tomography indication; checking nodes for metastases is a contrast indication.
Computed tomography with contrast
Correct. Metastases are an indication for contrast: it is good for showing involved lymph nodes, which are very numerous in the neck.
A lung-window scan alone
The lung window shows lung tissue in detail; lymph nodes for metastases are a contrast indication.

set2.io: Compare and contrast imaging modalities used in pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 48-year-old woman has sudden pleuritic chest pain, and pulmonary embolism is suspected. Which study is ordered first?
opts: A chest radiograph
The radiograph is first line for nearly everything else, but for suspected pulmonary embolism the angiogram is ordered first.
A ventilation/perfusion scan
The ventilation/perfusion scan is inferior to the angiogram; it is used when the angiogram cannot be done, mainly for contrast allergy.
Magnetic resonance imaging
Magnetic resonance is a secondary choice for vascular assessment; the angiogram is first for suspected pulmonary embolism.
A computed tomography angiogram
Correct. Suspected pulmonary embolism is the one case where computed tomography comes before the radiograph: a computed tomography angiogram.

mis.A chest radiograph: usual first test applied to the exception
